cim: Evaluating: “A Framework for America’s AI Future”
cim_eredeti: Evaluating: “A Framework for America’s AI Future”
szoveg_eredeti:
This bill package would hamper American AI development. While certain bills have interesting implications, Warner’s framework would be unlikely to advance American competitiveness in the global AI field.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the 21st century’s industrial revolution and is already fundamentally altering American life. Politicians are offering expansive and prescriptive frameworks for the still-emerging AI industry. While it is important to create an appropriate legal and regulatory framework for AI, many of these policies are overbroad retreads of age-old agendas of state expansion. This report examines Senator Mark Warner’s proposal, “A Framework for America’s AI Future,” which encompasses several bills, including:

This bill package would hamper American AI development. While certain bills have interesting implications, Warner’s framework would be unlikely to advance American competitiveness in the global AI field.

The Data Center Tax Accountability and Disclosure Act (DCTADA) is a combination of environmental mandates masquerading as thoughtful data center regulations. It would deny full and immediate expensing for equipment and machinery to most data centers. Full and immediate expensing or “100% bonus depreciation” was enacted temporarily in 2017 and made permanent in 2025. It allows companies, when calculating their taxable income, to deduct legitimate costs associated with equipment and machinery in the same year that they are placed in service, instead of spreading such deductions out across a prescribed “useful life” of the equipment. This is the proper tax treatment and consistent with how virtually all other legitimate business expenses are treated. By denying full and immediate expensing specifically to data centers, the DCTADA would discourage data center investments and would threaten America’s edge over China in the data center and AI development race.

The DCTADA carves out an exception that would allow full and immediate expensing for data centers that have a Gold or Platinum LEED Green Building certification. This would empower the U.S. Green Building Council (USGBC) to act as the arbiter of which data center projects can qualify for equal tax treatment and would push more companies to jump through the bureaucratic hoops established by USGBC. The carveout for “green” data centers suggests that the push to curtail AI and data centers in this legislation is being guided not by national security concerns, but by a desire to pick winners and losers and establish federal control over the industry.

The legislation would also impose an onerous reporting and disclosure regime over data centers. The reporting and disclosure would cover water access and usage, electricity access and usage, backup power usage, greenhouse gas emissions, etc. Companies that fail to comply with the reporting and disclosure requirements would be subject to stiff monetary penalties. This would further stifle data center development by diverting companies’ focus away from building, operations, and maintenance to the preparation of reports for government bureaucrats.

This bill is unnecessary because the private sector is already taking voluntary actions to use resources more efficiently and invest in carbon-free energy. Hyperscalers are signing long-term contracts and making investments to expand, restart, or preserve nuclear power plants and other carbon-free power projects to meet their growing data-center demand. An increasing number of newer facilities are also conserving water by adopting closed-loop cooling systems that reuse the same water within the data center. These voluntary initiatives avoid the unnecessary compliance costs associated with a government-directed “green energy” agenda that makes digital services and AI more expensive.

The AI AGENT Act requires large online platforms (defined as an online service with more than 50 million monthly customers or subscribers in the U.S.) to create pathways for AI agents to manage users’ online interactions, electronic commerce decisions, user-generated content, and account settings as if the agent were the user itself.

Platforms must maintain third-party accessible interfaces to allow an external user’s agent hosted and operated on another service to interact with the covered platform. Furthermore, the Act's definition of user data for social media platforms expressly includes “social graph data,” defined as the user's own content, their responses to others' content (explicitly excluding third-party users' content), public profile, and metadata. Companies that fail to comply with the Act face civil penalties for each user.

The Act requires that AI agent providers register with the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) before being allowed to access a large platform’s agent pathway. The Act imposes a duty on large platforms to provide access on fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory (FRAND) terms, with the FTC empowered to review fees and access denials.

The Act is government overreach that would force companies to invest significant resources in creating products without demand instead of focusing on what their customers want.

Allowing AI agents to interact with platforms on a user’s behalf has strong merit and may become the standard way accounts are managed in the future. For example, agents may become the most powerful and effective vehicle for parental account management for minors. However, this bill puts the cart before the horse and creates an onerous regulatory environment for a future that might not exist. AI agents are not sufficiently consistent at meeting many of the requirements imposed by the Act. Likewise, many large online platforms have legitimate competition, privacy, and intellectual property constraints that may be violated by forced access to their services.

A better way would be to allow this kind of data management as an option provided to an end user for a specific kind of data or service rather than to force it upon online services with a sufficiently large userbase. At the very least, a cleaner version of this Act with less FTC involvement, less strict penalties for violations, a restricted industry domain, and explicit good-faith safe harbors for both platforms and agent providers would likely solve many of these detriments.

The SAFE AI Act prohibits federal agencies from purchasing or using an AI image- or video-generating model that an agency head, the Administrator of General Services, or a federal court has determined fails safeguard standards against generating child sexual abuse material (CSAM) or non-consensual intimate images of identifiable adults (NCII).

The Act also prohibits offering tools primarily designed to circumvent, remove, or tamper with a model's technical controls, and creates a private right of action for an individual whose likeness is contained in any CSAM, an individual injured by a developer failing to implement sufficiently robust technical controls to prevent their likeness from being so used, and a developer whose technical controls are subverted.

The SAFE AI Act attempts to address AI-generated CSAM and NCII by limiting the federal government's ability to purchase services from vendors whose models produce them. This governmental apparatus would wield power as a consumer rather than a regulator to address a problem within a market.

The Act's construction may effectively bar government access to open-source and open-weight models, because their safeguards can be removed by parties the original developer does not control and because anyone who contributes to the open-source model is swept into its developer liability.
